To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) NAT1 and NAT 2 are the two human genes that encode N-acetyltransfer-ase proteins; 2) NAT1 and 2 are different in their substrate specificity, and in their stability; 3) NAT2 is the locus of the acetylator polymorphism; and 4) the acetyltransferase reaction can be used to predict the potential for arylamine-induced carcinogenesis in humans.
we have cloned and expressed the genes for two human arylamine-N-acetyltransferase isoforms, NAT1 and 2, which differ from each other with respect to their substrate specificity and stability.
we have identified the gene for the slow acetylator phenotype, and we have shown how to predict whether any arylamine will or will not be polymorphically N-acetylated.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the genetic and molecular basis of human arylamine acetylation polymorphisms, a major factor in the susceptibility of individuals to certain environmental carcinogens.
the molecular basis of a genetically determined variation of N-acetyltransferse enzyme activity in human populations.
the identification and characterization of the human genes that encode the N-acetyltransferas enzymes that catalyze the acetylation of arylamine drugs, carcinogens, and environmental pollutants.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the human acetylator gene polymorphism is due to the NAT2 gene.
NAT2 is responsible for the human arylamine acetylation polymorphisms and that NAT1 is not.

there is a single NAT2 gene, which encodes a protein (NAT2) that is the site of a human acetylator polymorphism and that there is a second gene (NAT1) that encodes an enzyme (NAT1), which is not the site of an acetylator polymorphic locus
